results.question: how long do i keep tax records
results.answer:
You should keep your tax records for the length of time that the IRS can legally examine them. The periods used in the U.S. tax system are in the “period of limitations” table and the specific rules for certain types of records.  

| Type of record | Retention period | Source |
|----------------|------------------|--------|
| General tax‑return records (income, deductions, credits) | Keep until the period of limitations for the return expires. For most income‑tax returns the default limitation is **3 years** from the date the return was filed, **4 years** if the return was filed on time and you made a **$1,000 or more** tax payment, or **7 years** if a tax was **under‑reported or you filed a fraudulent return**. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16) |
| Employment‑tax records (e.g., Forms 941, wage records, payroll taxes) | Keep **at least 4 years** after the date the tax becomes due or is paid – whichever is later. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16) |
| Asset‑related records (depreciation, basis, sale of property) | Keep until the limitation period expires for the year in which the property was disposed of, because you may need them to calculate depreciation, amortization, depletion, and gain/loss. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16) |
| Records needed for a refund claim | Keep **7 years** from the date the original return was due (not including extensions) or **2 years** from the date you paid the tax, whichever is later. | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=34) |
| General record‑keeping reminder | “What records must I keep? How long must I keep them?” – see the IRS guidance on record‑keeping. | [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=2) |

**Bottom line:**  
- For most ordinary tax‑return records, keep them for at least 3 years, but be prepared to keep them up to 7 years if a problem arises.  
- Keep employment‑tax records for 4 years.  
- Keep asset‑related records as long as the period of limitations for the year of disposal.  
- Keep any records you might need for a refund claim for 7 years or 2 years after payment.



**Sources:**
1. [irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf (Page 16)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)
2. [irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 34)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=34)

results.question: why do i need to keep business records
results.answer:
You need to keep business records because they serve several critical purposes for the day‑to‑day operation of your business and for compliance with tax and other government requirements.

* **Track performance** – Good records let you see whether the business is improving, which items sell well, and what changes are needed. This “monitor the progress of your business” part of keeping records can increase the likelihood of success. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)  
* **Prepare accurate financial statements** – Income (profit‑and‑loss) statements and balance sheets can only be created with solid records. These statements are used when dealing with banks or creditors and help you manage the business. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)  
* **Identify sources of receipts** – Your records show where money or property comes from, separating business from non‑business receipts and taxable from nontaxable income. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)  
* **Track deductible expenses** – If you record expenses when they occur, you are less likely to forget them when preparing a tax return. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)  
* **Prepare tax returns** – The same records that show income, deductions, and credits are required when you file tax returns. The IRS can require you to substantiate items reported on the return, and a complete set of records speeds up any examination. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)  
* **Support taxes and other legal filings** – In addition to federal tax records, you must keep records for other filings such as payroll, employment taxes, and, in some states, business name registrations. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=6)  

These reasons are reinforced in later segments: a proper record‑keeping system must show gross income and deductions, be kept in both hard‑copy and electronic format, and be maintained for as long as the IRS could need them. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)  

In short, keeping records lets you track how the business performs, ensures you can provide accurate financial statements and tax returns, and keeps you ready for any IRS or government review.



**Sources:**

results.question: how do i check my workplace for hazards
results.answer:
To identify and control hazards in your workplace, follow the steps that the handbook recommends for a routine **workplace self‑inspection**:

| What to do | How to do it | Where the guidance comes from |
|------------|--------------|--------------------------------|
| **1. Plan the inspection** – decide when and how often it will happen, who will lead it, and what areas will be covered. | Use the Self‑Inspection Checklist in the handbook as a starting point. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8) |
| **2. Inspect each area of the worksite** – walk the floors, look at equipment, machines and any confined spaces. | Workers can help spot things that owners or supervisors might miss. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8) |
| **3. Identify hazards** – note anything that could harm a worker (exposed wires, slip‑prone floors, chemical containers, etc.). | The checklist items (e.g., “walking‑working surfaces,” “hazardous chemicals,” “confined spaces”) help you remember the common hazard classes. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8) |
| **4. Control the hazards** – decide which control is best (engineering, administrative, PPE). | After an issue is found, the checklist indicates actions like adding guardrails, sealing containers, or posting warnings. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8) |
| **5. Monitor and evaluate** – after controls are in place, keep checking to make sure they keep working. | Keep a log of inspections, repairs, and any incidents that occur afterward. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8) |
| **6. Compile the data** – combine the completed checklists with injury/illness records, training logs, and maintenance records. | This gives a full picture of where problems dwell and what solutions still need work. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8) |
| **7. Match the findings to OSHA standards** – if a hazard is regulated, check the standard to make sure you are meeting the requirements. | Review the “Subpart” and the “hazard” references noted on the checklist to see the applicable regulation. | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=91) |
| **8. Get help if you need it** – use the free, confidential On‑Site Consultation Program to get expert help in spotting or fixing hazards. | The consultation can be a single‑issue visit or a full‑facility review. | [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=90) |
| **9. Keep the program alive** – update the checklist, retrain workers, and adjust controls when the work environment changes. | The handbook says the program is a living part of everyday work life. | [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=5) |

**Practical example**

*You’re a small café owner.  
1. You schedule a monthly walk‑through with the baristas.  
2. Using the checklist page for “Walk‑working surfaces” (Segments 12 or 16), you spot a wet spill in the back‑counter area.  
3. You note the spill as a slipping hazard, add a warning sign, and clean the area immediately.  
4. The next inspection shows the spill was cleaned; the control is working.  
5. You add the case to a “hazard log” that also records previous slips (from the OSHA 300 log).*

**Key take‑away**

- **Inspect regularly, involve workers, and use the handbook’s checklists to spot hazards.**  
- **Control the hazards, monitor them, and keep a record.**  
- **Use OSHA resources (standards, videos, publications) and, if needed, the On‑Site Consultation Program for expert help.**

These steps are the only ones the provided segments give for checking your workplace for hazards.

results.question: cash or accrual accounting whats the difference
results.answer:
Cash accounting and accrual accounting differ mainly in **when income and expenses are recognized**.

|  | Cash method | Accrual method |
|---|---|---|
| **Income** | Included when you actually receive it (or when it is constructively received). Example: a check issued on December 30, 2024 but received on January 4, 2025 is counted in 2025 income. | Included when you earn it—when the right to receive and the amount can be determined, even if payment comes later. Example: you sell a computer on December 28, 2025 but bill in January 2026 and receive payment in February 2026; the sale is still reported as 2025 income. | 
| **Expenses** | Deducted or capitalized in the year you pay them. | Deducted or capitalized in the year you incur them, regardless of when you actually pay. |
| **Purpose** | Records cash flow – easier to use for simple businesses. | Matches income with the expenses that caused it – provides a clearer picture of profitability. |
| **Inventory rule** | If inventory is involved you *usually* must use the accrual method unless you qualify as a small‑business taxpayer. | Same rule: inventory requires accrual unless you qualify as a small‑business taxpayer. |

Key points from the IRS guidance:

* Cash method: “include in your gross income all items of income you actually or constructively receive during your tax year” – *constructive receipt* means the amount is available to you even if you don’t take possession yet [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14).  
* Accrual method: “you generally include an amount in your gross income for the tax year in which all events that fix your right to receive the income have occurred” and you can deduct expenses in the year the liability is fixed, even if payment is later [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15)[[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16).  
* Inventory and purchase/sale of merchandise generally require the accrual method unless you are a small‑business taxpayer. The IRS specifies this in the “Choosing an Accounting Method” instructions [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5), and again in the inventory discussion [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14).

Thus, the core difference is that **cash accounting reports income when it’s received and expenses when paid, while accrual accounting reports income when earned and expenses when incurred**. This distinction affects when transactions are included in your tax year and can also require you to use different bookkeeping methods, especially if you keep inventory.



**Sources:**
1. [irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 14)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)
2. [irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 15)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15)

results.question: can i deduct business travel
results.answer:
Yes, you can deduct reasonable and necessary business‑travel expenses.  
**What you can deduct**

* **Transportation** – The cost of air, train, bus, or car travel between your home (or “tax home”) and a temporary work location. This also includes airfare, taxis, commuter buses, limousines, tolls and parking fees you incur between the airport or station and your hotel or between the hotel and the work site.   [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40)  
* **Meals** – If the trip requires an overnight stay or is long enough that you need sleep or rest to perform your duties, you may deduct the cost of meals.  You can take either the actual expenses or the standard meal allowance, but in most cases you can only deduct 50 % of the meal expenses.  [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41)  
* **Lodging** – Hotel or other overnight accommodations are deductible under the same circumstances as meals.  [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41)  
* **Other related expenses** – Dry‑cleaning and laundry while traveling, telephone or fax communication used for business, tips paid for any of the above items, and costs of business calls made while on the trip.  [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41)  
* **Reimbursement to employees** – If you reimburse employees for travel or meal expenses, those reimbursements are generally deductible, depending on whether the plan is accountable or non‑accountable.  [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41)  

**Limits and rules**

* A deduction applies only to the **business‑use portion** of any expense; you must separate any personal use.  [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41)  
* If you use the **standard mileage rate** for car expenses while traveling, you cannot separately deduct car insurance premiums.  [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)  

In short, you may deduct transportation, meals (50 % of the costs), lodging, and related items incurred while traveling away from home for business, as laid out in Pub. 463 and reiterated in the excerpts above.



**Sources:**
1. [irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 40)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40)
2. [irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 41)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41)
3. [irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf (Page 11)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)

results.question: what goes in an executive summary
results.answer:
An executive summary is a concise snapshot of the entire business plan. It should include:

* **Your business idea** – a clear, one‑to‑two‑sentence overview of what you’re offering.  
* **Capital requirements** – the total amount of money you need, why you need it, and how you’ll use it.  
* **Owner or investor contribution** – the cash, equipment, or other assets you or other stakeholders are putting into the venture.  
* **Financial highlights** – a brief note on expected revenue, profits, or cash flow (often from the first year or three‑year projection).  
* **Milestone schedule** – a short timeline of key goals (product launch, first sales, breakeven, etc.).  

These elements are written after the full plan is completed so they can reflect the final facts and figures.  

[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)



**Sources:**
1. [sba_business_planning_guide.pdf (Page 4)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)

results.question: how do i describe my target market
results.answer:
To describe your target market you should follow the steps outlined in the plan guide:

1. **Define the niche** – state exactly what product or service you will offer and why it matters to a specific group of customers.  
   - “Describe your market niche; who is your best customer.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

2. **Identify customer characteristics** – list the traits that make a customer a good fit.  
   - For business customers: industry, company size, location, product use.  
   - For consumers: demographics (age, gender), geographic location, economic status, lifestyle, product application or benefits sought. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

3. **Estimate size and growth potential** – use population figures, sales tax data, industry reports, etc., to project how large the market is and how fast it is growing.  
   - “Estimate the approximate size and growth potential of the target market(s) using population figures, sales tax info, industry information, etc.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

4. **Project market share** – decide how much of that total market you expect to capture.  
   - “Estimate how much of the total market you will capture.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

5. **Use the information later in the plan** – when you write your “Marketing” section, reference this target‑market description to explain how you will reach them and how you will position your product or service. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=15)  

By combining these elements you’ll have a clear, data‑driven description of who your best customers are, where they live or operate, what drives their buying, and how big the opportunity is.



**Sources:**
1. [sba_business_planning_guide.pdf (Page 14)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)
2. [sba_business_planning_guide.pdf (Page 15)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=15)

results.question: do i have to make my shop wheelchair accessible
results.answer:
Yes.  
If your shop serves the public, the Americans with Disabilities Act requires you to remove any “barriers” that are **readily achievable** so that people who use wheelchairs (and other disabilities) can access your premises. The ADA does not mandate that every business be 100 % compliant, but it does require removing physically obvious barriers whenever that can be done without excessive cost or hardship.  

‑ “If you own or operate a business that serves the public you must remove physical ‘barriers’ that are ‘readily achievable,’” which means you must take steps to make the place usable for wheelchair users wherever it is reasonably possible.  
‑ Where full compliance is impractical, the law gives some leeway, particularly for existing facilities built before 1993, but the minimal requirement remains: eliminate any clearly definable, easily solvable obstacles to access.  

So, if you run a shop open to the public, you are required to make it wheelchair‑accessible to the extent that the barriers are readily achievable. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6)



**Sources:**
1. [ada_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 6)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6)

results.question: how long do i have to report a workplace death
results.answer:
All work‑related fatalities must be reported to OSHA within 8 hours of the death.

results.question: am i exempt from injury recordkeeping
results.answer:
You are **partially exempt** from OSHA’s injury‑and‑illness recordkeeping rules if **both** of the following conditions are true:

* **Your employer has 10 or fewer employees for the entire last calendar year** — see 29 CFR 1904.1 [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14)  
* OR **you work in a low‑hazard industry listed in 29 CFR Part 1904, Subpart B, Appendix A** [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14)

Even when exempt, you still must:

* **Report all work‑related fatalities, in‑patient hospitalizations, amputations, and loss of an eye** to OSHA within the required time frames (8 hours for fatality, 24 hours for hospitalization, amputation, or loss of an eye) [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15)  
* **Keep injury and illness records (OSHA Form 300, 301, and 300A) at the worksite for at least five years** [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15)  

If you do **not** meet the exemption criteria, you must keep and report the records as described in the OSHA regulations.

results.question: how long do i keep injury records
results.answer:
In the U.S., employers who must keep OSHA injury and illness records are required to retain the logs (OSHA Form 300, 300A and 301) at the worksite for **at least five (5) years** [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15).  

If a worker’s medical or exposure record is also required to be kept, the retention period is the time required for that specific type of record [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15).

results.question: what records do i keep for tax and for injuries and for how long
results.answer:
**What to keep for tax**

- All documents that support the income, expenses, or deductions shown on your tax return must be kept until the “period of limitations” for that return expires.  The statute of limitations is the same time that you could still claim a refund or the IRS could still assess additional tax.  Generally this is **7 years from the date your original return was due** (extensions are not counted).  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=34)  
- If you have employees, you must keep employment‑tax records (W‑2s, payroll ledgers, tax‑paying documents, etc.) for at least **4 years after the date the tax becomes due or is paid, whichever is later**.  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)  
- For any property that you own and later dispose of, retain the records that show your basis, depreciation, and proceeds until the year in which you dispose of it is past its period of limitations.  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)  

**What to keep for injuries (OSHA requirements)**

- All occupational injuries or illnesses that are “recordable” must be logged on **OSHA Form 300 (Log of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses)**, and each recordable event gets a separate **OSHA Form 301 (Incident Report)**.  These records must be kept at the worksite for at least **five (5) years** after the record‑keeping date.  [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15)  
- Annual summaries of injuries/illnesses are prepared on **OSHA Form 300A (Summary of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses)**.  OSHA requires that the records be electronically submitted by March 2 of the year following the calendar year covered, if you have 100 + workers in a high‑hazard industry. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15)  
- Worker medical and exposure records are retained for the period required by the specific type of record, and training records must be kept and accessible for OSHA review as required.  [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15)  

**Bottom line**

| Purpose | Records to keep | Retention period |
|---------|-----------------|------------------|
| Income & deductions on tax returns | Amounts, receipts, invoices, bank statements, payroll ledgers, etc. | Until the period of limitations expires (usually 7 years from the original return’s due date) |
| Employment tax records | W‑2s, 941s, payroll records, tax‑payment receipts | ≥ 4 years after the tax due or paid date |
| Business assets | Purchase invoices, depreciation schedules, sale documents | Until the disposal year’s period of limitations ends |
| OSHA injury/illness logs | Form 300, Form 301, Form 300A | ≥ 5 years at the worksite; electronic submission by March 2 if required |
| Medical & exposure records | Work‑related medical records, exposure logs | Retained for the time required by the specific record category |
| Training records | OSHA‑approved training logs | Must remain accessible for OSHA review as required |

These are the only record‑keeping requirements mentioned in the provided documents.



**Sources:**
1. [irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf (Page 16)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)
2. [irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 34)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=34)
3. [osha_small_business_handbook.pdf (Page 15)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15)

results.question: how do i start a business and keep my taxes organized
results.answer:
**Starting a Business**

1. Choose a legal structure (sole proprietorship, partnership, corporation, LLC, etc.).  The type you pick determines the tax forms you’ll file and the paperwork you’ll need to file with the state.  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=2)  
2. If you’ll be paid under a name that isn’t your own last name, file a **fictitious‑name** statement with the county Register of Deeds or the Secretary of State’s office.  This gives your business exclusive use of that name.  [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=6)  
3. File the appropriate incorporation documents:
   * **Corporation** – file articles of incorporation and obtain a Certificate of Incorporation.  
   * **LLC** – file articles of organization.  
   These steps are required if you choose to incorporate or form an LLC.  [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=6)  
4. Obtain an **Employer Identification Number (EIN)** from the IRS (even if you have no employees, an EIN is an alternative to using your SSN).  A new EIN automatically enrolls you in the Electronic Federal Tax Payment System (EFTPS).  [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6), [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=6)  
5. Decide on an accounting **method** and a **tax year**.  
   * For most small businesses, the **cash method** is simplest, but you may use accrual if it better reflects your activity.  [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)  
   * The **tax year** can be a calendar year (Jan 1 – Dec 31) or a fiscal year ending on any month‑except‑December.  Once chosen, you must keep your books for that period and, if you change later, file Form 1128 for IRS approval.  [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)  
6. Open a **business checking account** and keep it separate from personal accounts.  Day‑to‑day receipts and checks should be deposited here, and the account should be reconciled regularly.  [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=14)  

**Keeping Your Taxes Organized**

1. Maintain a **record‑keeping system** that includes:
   * a business checkbook (or electronic check‑book if you prefer),  
   * a daily summary of cash receipts,  
   * a monthly summary of cash receipts,  
   * a check‑disbursement journal,  
   * ledgers or journals that total each account,  
   * copies of all receipts, invoices, and bank statements.  [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=14), [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=13)  

2. Record each transaction **as it happens** and label the source of income or expense so you can separate business from non‑business items.  [[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)  
3. Keep **supporting documents** for every entry: credit‑card sales slips, purchase orders, receipts, and, for cash payments, a written explanation if no receipt exists.  [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=13)  

4. Use **electronic records** if desired.  The IRS accepts electronic copies provided the system can index, store, preserve, retrieve, and reproduce the records in a legible format and give the IRS access when needed.  [[9]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)  

5. Understand **who and what you must report**:  
   * Income over \$600 to a contractor requires a Form 1099‑MISC or 1099‑NEC, filed by Jan 31 each year.  
   * Employees require Forms W‑2 (and to the IRS, a Form W‑3), and wages must be reported on Form 940 if the business is a payor of federal employment taxes.  [[10]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=13)  
   * If you have other obligations (e.g., excise taxes, VAT, etc.), check the applicable tables for due dates and forms.  [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6)  

6. Pay **estimated taxes** if you expect at least \$1,000 in tax liability (sole proprietors, partners, S‑corp shareholders) or \$500 if your corporation is liable.  Use Form 1040‑ES for individuals.  [[11]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=6)  

7. Keep records for the period required by the IRS (usually at least **3 years** for most tax returns; keep them longer if other agencies or creditors may need them).  [[12]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)  

**Putting It All Together**

Start by choosing your business type, filing the required formation documents, and getting an EIN.  Set up a dedicated bank account, decide on a tax year and accounting method, and open an organized record‑keeping system.  Record every transaction promptly, keep all supporting documents, and file the necessary information returns and tax payments on time.  This organized, documented approach will make filing your returns smoother, keep you ready for an IRS audit, and let you focus on growing your business.

results.question: what do i need to do to keep employees safe and my premises accessible
results.answer:
To keep **employees safe** and your **premises accessible** you need a coordinated approach that covers physical layout, equipment, policies, and emergency procedures. Below is a practical checklist you can apply immediately, with every item backed up by the handbook segments.

---

## 1    **Clear, safe walk‑working surfaces**

- Keep all walking‑working surfaces clean, dry, and free of obstructions.  
- Repair holes, cover gaps, and add non‑slip mats where wet.  
- Store materials so they do not block aisles.  
- Provide guardrails or safety nets on raised surfaces > 4 ft (≈ 1.2 m).  
- Inspect regularly and keep a record of hazards.  
  *[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=78)[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=79)[[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=73)*  

---

## 2    **Accessible entrances**

| Requirement | Detail | Citation |
|-------------|--------|----------|
| Ramp | Max slope 1:12, handrails if slope > 1:20 **and** rise > 6 in. | [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10) |
| Turnstile | Remove or replace with an accessible gate; opening ≥ 32 in wide. | [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=13) |
| Signage | If an inaccessible entrance exists, sign the accessible route. | [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10) |
| Security | If a door is locked for safety, install an accessible call box or buzzer (≤ 48 in high). | [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10) |
| Accessibility policy | Open accessible doors during business hours; allow staff to unlock if necessary. | [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=18) |

---

## 3    **Accessible parking**

| Feature | Detail | Citation |
|---------|--------|----------|
| Width | At least 8 ft (96 in). | [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=8) |
| Clear vertical clearance | 98 in from ground to vehicle roof. | [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=8) |
| Access aisle | 8 ft wide, 1:50 slope max, level ground. | [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=8) |
| Signage | International symbol + “VAN ACCESSIBLE” high enough to see. | [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=8) |
| Van‑accessible spaces | 1/8 of total spaces if > 8; at least one van‑accessible if only one space. | [[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=9) |
| Proximity | Locate within a clearly marked accessible route to the building. | [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=8) |

---

## 4    **Accessible inside layout**

### a. Counters & service areas
| Requirement | Detail | Citation |
|-------------|--------|----------|
| Counter height | Max 34 in above floor; lip ≤ 38 in (40 in with lip). | [[9]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15) |
| Accessible aisle | Minimum 36 in wide, clearly marked with the international symbol. | [[9]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15) |
| Lowered section | ≥ 60 in long, ≤ 34 in high. | [[10]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16) |
| Assistive service | If accessibility is not feasible, offer alternate service (e.g., staff assists). | [[10]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16) |

### b. Seating & tables
| Requirement | Detail | Citation |
|-------------|--------|----------|
| Table height | 28–34 in; knee clearance 27 in. | [[11]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=17) |
| Accessible seating | At least 30 in × 48 in clear floor space; reachable from an accessible route. | [[11]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=17) |
| Fixed tables | At least 5 % of tables (or ≥ 1 if fewer than 20) must be accessible when readily achievable. | [[11]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=17) |

### c. Mail & other service points
- Provide a low‑height mailbox or front counter spot for the ADA‑eligible customers.  
  *[[12]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=59)*

---

## 5    **Emergency exits & evacuation**

- All required exits must be unobstructed, side‑hinged, and open from the exit direction with ≤ 15‑lb force.  
- No revolving or sliding doors as required exits.  
- Exit signs: minimum 6 in tall, lettering ¾ in wide, illuminated.  
- Clear exit paths marked with “EXIT” or “NOT AN EXIT” where needed.  
- Provide emergency lighting that lasts 30 s monthly, 90 min yearly.  
  *[[13]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=23)[[14]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=28)*  

- **Emergency plan** must:  
  - Identify evacuation triggers, chain of command, and assembly area.  
  - Include instructions for assisting people with disabilities or those who don’t speak English.  
  - Account for visitors and employees alike.  
  *[[15]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=26)*

---

## 6

results.question: do i need an ein and what accounting method comes with it
results.answer:
Yes. If your business is a sole proprietorship, partnership, LLC, or corporation, you normally need an Employer Identification Number (EIN) so the IRS can process your tax filings and any payroll or excise‑tax returns you must file [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=4). You can apply for an EIN online by visiting IRS.gov/EIN or by submitting Form SS‑4 [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=4).

When you file your first income‑tax return you also choose an accounting method for the business [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5). The IRS allows two basic methods:

* **Cash method** – income is reported in the year you receive it, and expenses are deducted or capitalized in the year you pay them [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5).
* **Accrual method** – income is reported in the year it is earned, even if payment comes later, and expenses are deducted or capitalized in the year they are incurred [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5).

You choose either method at the time of your first return; there is no required accounting method that “comes with” an EIN. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14) also explains that you may use either method (or a combination method) as long as it consistently reflects income and expenses for the tax year.



**Sources:**

results.question: what forms do i keep for injuries and how long do i keep them
results.answer:
For workplace injuries you must keep the OSHA injury‑record forms the employer is required to complete:

* **OSHA Form 300 – Log of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses** (records every recordable injury or illness).  
* **OSHA Form 301 – Injury and Illness Incident Report** (a detailed report for each recordable case).  
* **OSHA Form 300A – Summary of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses** (the annual summary filed after the calendar year ends).

The employer must keep these records at the worksite **for at least five years** after the date they were created.  That five‑year retention period applies to the injury and illness records themselves; other records (e.g., medical or exposure records) may have their own specific retention times, but for injuries the required forms must be retained for **five years** [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15).

results.answer:
Yes.  
- **Requirement:** Workers’ compensation insurance is required by state law whenever you have employees, to cover any bodily‑injury or job‑related disease claims. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=37)

results.question: what do i file for my employees and what state taxes do i owe for them
results.answer:
You’ll need to file a handful of federal forms that report what you pay your employees and the taxes you withhold, and you’ll also be required to pay state‑level payroll taxes (at least the state unemployment fund and, in most states, state income‑tax withholding).  The context below gives the specific federal forms you must file and the state‑level tax that is mentioned.

| What you file | Why you file | Reference |
|--------------|--------------|-----------|
| **Form W‑2** – Wage and Tax Statement | Reports each employee’s wages, tips, withheld federal income tax, Social Security and Medicare taxes, and the amounts you pay on their behalf.  Employers must give a copy to the employee and file a copy with the Social Security Administration. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=9) |
| **Form W‑3** – Transmittal of Forms W‑2 | A summary of all W‑2s you file for the year. | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=13) |
| **Form 941** – Employer’s QUARTERLY Federal Tax Return (or **Form 944** – ANNUAL) | Reports quarterly amounts withheld for federal income tax, Social Security and Medicare taxes, and your employer’s share of those payroll taxes. | [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=7) |
| **Form 940** – Employer’s Annual Federal Unemployment (FUTA) Tax Return | Reports the federal unemployment tax you pay (no employee share). | [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=7) |
| **Form I‑9** | Verifies that each employee is legally eligible to work in the U.S.; required before you can withhold taxes. | [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=7) |
| **Form W‑4** | Employee completes this so you can compute the correct amount of federal income tax to withhold. | [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=7) |

### State‑level payroll taxes

* **State Unemployment Insurance (SUI) tax** – Employers must make quarterly contributions to the state’s unemployment insurance fund.  For example, in South Dakota the employer contributes to the **State Unemployment Tax** and you can find the department contact and required reporting windows in the state labor office.  The contribution rate and due dates are set by the state; the employer is the sole payer. | [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=9) |

> *What’s missing:* The segments do not provide the exact rates or due dates for other state taxes such as state income‑tax withholding, state disability insurance, or other state‑specific payroll taxes. You’ll need to check your state’s labor or revenue department for those details.

**Bottom line**  
- File **W‑2/W‑3**, **941** or **944**, **940**, **I‑9** and **W‑4** for each employee.  
- Pay the state unemployment tax (and any other state‑specific payroll taxes that apply).  
- For details on rates, deadlines, and any additional state filing requirements, consult the tax department (or the “State Unemployment Tax” guidance in your state’s labor office).

results.question: what if a customer cannot get through my front door and what if someone is hurt on site
results.answer:
**If a customer cannot get through my front door**

- The ADA requires that *at least one* entrance be accessible.  If the front door is not accessible, you must provide and keep open an alternate accessible entrance at all business hours.  A clear sign must direct customers to that entrance.  The sign must be visible and readable. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10)  
- If the barrier is a turnstile or other gate, you must either remove it or replace it with an accessible gate that provides at least a 32‑inch opening, or point customers to an existing accessible door. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=13)

**If someone is hurt on site**

- First aid: A fully supplied first‑aid kit must be easily accessible in each work area, and at least one employee on each shift must be trained to give first aid. If the workplace lacks a nearby medical facility, at least one employee must be qualified for first aid, and if the employee’s role includes responding to emergencies, they should have received additional training and hepatitis‑B vaccination. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=62)  
- Emergency action plan: The plan must identify evacuation conditions, a chain of command, evacuation routes, and procedures for assisting people with disabilities or who do not speak English. It must also include procedures for accounting for workers and visitors after evacuation. [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=26)  
- Injury recording: Any injury that requires more than first help must be logged on OSHA Form 300, a detailed incident report on Form 301, and an annual summary on Form 300A.  Employers with 10 or fewer workers may be partially exempt, but still must report fatalities, hospitalizations, amputations, and eye loss. [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14)  
- General safety: Work‐site walking surfaces must be kept clean, free of hazards, and have adequate guardrails for elevated areas.  A good emergency exit network and visible exit signs are also required. [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=79)[[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=78)[[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=28)

These guidelines come directly from the small‑business safety and health handbook and address both parts of the question.

results.question: why should i bother with a safety program and what records do i need to keep
results.answer:
People who put a safety program in place usually see **fewer injuries, lower insurance costs, and happier workers**.  OSHA’s own data show that a well‑run program can cut injury rates and keep a business from costly investigations or penalties.  Having a program also helps you **avoid future losses** – inspections are smoother, workers stay healthier, and the business stays “sound” in the long run.  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=6)

### What types of records must you keep?

| Record | What it covers | How long you must keep it | Note |
|--------|----------------|---------------------------|------|
| **OSHA Form 300 (Log of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses)** | Any injury or illness that requires first aid, causes loss of a workday, or meets other criteria | **5 years** at the worksite | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |
| **OSHA Form 301 (Injury and Illness Incident Report)** | Detailed report for each recordable case | **5 years** at the worksite (same as Form 300) | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |
| **OSHA Form 300‑A (Summary of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses)** | Annual summary of the year’s 300/301 data | **5 years** at the worksite | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |
| **Electronic submission to OSHA** | Upload 300/301 data if you’re a 100‑plus‑worker high‑hazard business | Submit **by March 2** of the year after the calendar year covered | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |
| **Worker medical and exposure records** | Health records for employees exposed to hazards | Retain for the period required by the specific record type (varies by exposure) | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |
| **Worker training records** | Proof that workers were trained on safety and hazards | Keep available for **review by workers** as required | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |
| **Fatalities, hospitalizations, amputations, eye loss** | Must be reported to OSHA at the time of event | **Within 8 hours** for fatalities; **within 24 hours** for hospitalizations, amputations, or eye loss | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |
| **Infection‑related incidents** | Record infectious diseases and fatalities | Same timing as general fatalities and hospitalizations (8 h for fatality, 24 h for hospitalization) | [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=48) |
| **Other OSHA‑specific records** | Depending on your industry, may include lock‑out/tag‑out logs, respirator programs, noise‑monitoring logs, etc. | Keep as long as applicable (often 5 years) | [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=50), [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=64) |

### Quick checklist of common safety‑related records

- **Incident logs (Forms 300/301)** – keep for 5 years.  
- **Annual summary (Form 300‑A)** – keep for 5 years.  
- **Training certificates** – keep as long as the training is required.  
- **Medical/health screening records** – keep for the required period (often years, depending on exposure).  
- **Special injury types (infectious disease, noise‑induced hearing loss, etc.)** – record on Forms 300/301 and keep for 5 years.  

If you’re a small shop with fewer than 10 workers overall last year, you may be **partially exempt** from some injury/illness recordkeeping but you still must **report** any fatalities, hospitalizations, amputations, and eye loss.  [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14)

---

**Bottom line:**  
1. A safety program saves money and protects people.  
2. Keep injury/illness logs, incident reports, and annual summaries for **5 years**; file electronic copies by **March 2** if required; report serious events within **8 or 24 hours**.  
3. Maintain training, medical, and other OSHA‑specific records for the periods required by law (usually 5 years or whatever the specific regulation says).  

These records not only help you stay compliant, but they give you the data you need to spot problems, improve procedures, and keep your business safe and successful.  [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15)[[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14)[[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=48)

results.question: how do i register a trademark
results.answer:
To register a trademark, you can choose either a **state‑level** or a **federal (U.S. Patent and Trademark Office, USPTO) registration**.  
1. **Decide where to register** – state registration gives you rights only within that state, while federal registration gives nationwide protection.  
2. **Search the trademark database first** to make sure the mark you want isn’t already taken [[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=10)(http://sdsos.gov/)] (you can do this through the Secretary of State’s site or the USPTO website).  
3. **File the application**:  
   * **State filing** – submit through the Secretary of State in your state; e.g., in South Dakota you can call (605) 773‑2797 or visit https://sdsos.gov/.  
   * **Federal filing** – submit through the USPTO by calling (703) 308‑HELP or (800) 786‑9199, or use the USPTO website at www.uspto.gov.  

Follow the instructions on the appropriate website, include all required documents, and pay the filing fee. The agency will review and, if approved, issue the trademark registration.



**Sources:**
1. [sba_business_planning_guide.pdf (Page 10)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=10)

runs.question: how long do i keep tax records
runs.answer:
Keep the paperwork that backs up the income, deductions, and credits on each tax return for the amount of time the IRS could still look at that return – the “period of limitations.” That period starts on the return’s due date (or the filing date if filed late). In practice you should keep a copy of every return you file forever; the other supporting documents should stay until that period of limitations ends. In addition, the IRS gives specific, shorter time‑frames for certain kinds of records:  
* **Employment‑tax records** — keep them for at least 4 years after the tax became due or was paid, whichever is later.  
* **Property‑related records** — retain them until the period of limitations expires for the year in which you dispose of the property in a taxable disposition (so you can prove basis, depreciation, etc.).  

These rules come directly from the IRS guidance on record retention.  
[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)



**Sources:**
1. [irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf (Page 16)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)

runs.question: why do i need to keep business records
runs.answer:
You need to keep business records for several practical and legal reasons:

1. **Monitor the progress of your business** – Good records let you see whether the business is improving, which items sell best, and what changes are needed.  
   [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)  

2. **Prepare accurate financial statements** – Records are required to produce income (profit‑and‑loss) statements and balance sheets, which you need when dealing with banks or creditors and for managing the business.  
   [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)  

3. **Identify the source of receipts** – Knowing where money or property comes from helps you separate business from non‑business receipts and taxable from non‑taxable income.  
   [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)  

4. **Track deductible expenses** – Recording expenses promptly prevents forgetting them when you file your tax return.  
   [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)  

5. **Prepare tax returns** – You need the same records that support income, expenses, and credits reported on your return.  
   [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)  

6. **Support items reported on tax returns** – The IRS may examine any return and ask you to explain reported items; a complete record set speeds that inspection.  
   [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)  

These points cover all the reasons shown in the provided segments.

runs.question: what accounting method should i use
runs.answer:
You can choose among a few standard methods. The choice depends mainly on whether you keep inventory and how you want to match income with expenses.  
- **Cash method** – Report income when you receive it and deduct or capitalize expenses in the year you pay them. It is simplest and often used by small businesses that don’t keep inventory. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)]  
- **Accrual method** – Report income when it is earned (even if you don’t receive payment yet) and deduct or capitalize expenses in the year they are incurred. If you sell, produce, or purchase merchandise you must generally use accrual for those transactions, because you’ll need an inventory system to track costs of goods sold. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14), [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)]  
- **Special methods** – Certain items (e.g., amortization, depreciation, bad‑debt deduction, installment sales, long‑term contracts) have their own rules that can be combined with cash or accrual for the rest of the business. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=17)  
- **Combination method** – You may mix cash, accrual, and special methods as long as the overall system clearly shows your income and is used consistently. If the combination includes the cash method for either income or expenses, treat the whole set as the cash method. [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16)  

Once you file your first return (Schedule C on Form 1040) you must state your chosen method. If you later decide to change it, you generally need IRS approval—file Form 3115 or request a ruling with Form 1128. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=17)  

So pick the method that fits your inventory situation and how you prefer to match income with expenses. If you have inventory, choose accrual; otherwise cash is often easier. If you need to treat some items specially, combine accordingly.



**Sources:**
1. [irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 14)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)
2. [irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf (Page 5)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)

runs.question: how do i check my workplace for hazards
runs.answer:
To systematically find hazards in your workplace, use the procedure outlined in the handbook:

1. **Conduct routine self‑inspections**  
   * Have knowledgeable workers walk the worksite and review the *Self‑Inspection Checklists* that cover typical industry hazards.  
   * Identify any hazards, decide how to control them, and then monitor the controls to ensure they remain effective.  
   * The handbook notes that self‑inspections are the only way to know if hazards exist and are being managed.  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)

2. **Collect supporting information**  
   * Combine the checklist results with injury and illness records, worker training logs, maintenance logs, and incident reports.  
   * This combined data set helps you spot patterns and pinpoint where controls need improvement.  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)

3. **Match hazards to OSHA standards**  
   * For each potential hazard you find, review the relevant OSHA standard to see whether it applies to your work, equipment, or materials.  
   * If you’re unsure, consult the OSHA website or your local OSHA Area Office.  [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=91)

4. **Use OSHA resources and support**  
   * The handbook encourages using the *On‑Site Consultation Program*—free, confidential visits by trained safety consultants who can help you assess hazards and fix them.  
   * They also advise on compliance, training, and improving safety programs.  [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=90)

5. **Make inspection part of your safety program**  
   * Embed regular inspections in your overall safety and health program, involve workers, and keep records of inspections and corrective actions.  [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=7)

By following these steps—routine self‑inspections, data collection, standard review, and utilizing OSHA consultation—you can actively detect, control, and monitor workplace hazards.



**Sources:**

runs.question: cash or accrual accounting whats the difference
runs.answer:
Cash vs. accrual accounting

**Cash method**  
- Income is reported in the year you actually receive it or when it is constructively received (the money is available to you).  
- Expenses are deducted in the year you pay them.  
- It is simpler and is common for sole proprietors or small businesses that do not keep inventory.  
- Example: If you get a check in January for services performed in December, you report the income in the year you received the check (January’s tax year) [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14).

**Accrual method**  
- Income is reported in the year it is earned, even if payment comes later.  
- Expenses are deducted in the year they are incurred, regardless of when you actually pay them.  
- This method matches income with the expenses that produced it, giving a more accurate picture of profitability.  
- It is required when you keep inventory; inventories must be taken into account at the start and end of each tax year [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5) and [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15).

**Key differences**  

| Aspect | Cash method | Accrual method |
|--------|-------------|----------------|
|When income counts | When received or constructively received | When earned (when the right to receive is fixed) |
|When expenses count | When paid | When incurred |
|Inventory requirement | Can use if you have no inventory | Required if inventory is used [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5) |
|Matching principle | Not automatically matched | Matches income and expenses that belong in the same period [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15) |

So, cash accounting records money that actually moves in or out; accrual accounting records money that should have moved based on the business’s performance.



**Sources:**
1. [irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 14)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)
2. [irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf (Page 5)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)
3. [irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 15)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15)

runs.question: can i deduct business travel
runs.answer:
Yes.  
If the travel is for the purpose of carrying out your business, most of the related costs are deductible.

* **Transportation** – You may deduct the cost of travel by airplane, train, bus or car between your home and the business destination, as well as taxi, commuter‑bus or limousine fares between the airport (or train station) and your hotel or between the hotel and the work location. You can also deduct the cost of sending baggage or sample material between workplaces. These are covered under the “Transportation” section for business travel 【Segment 3】.  

* **Car or truck** – If you use your vehicle for the trip, you can deduct either the actual expenses (fuel, oil, repairs, insurance, parking, tolls, etc.) or the IRS‑announced standard mileage rate for that year. The deduction must be limited to the portion of the vehicle use that is for business. These rules are in the “Car and Truck Expenses” section 【Segment 5】.  

* **Meals and lodging** – You can deduct the cost of meals and lodging when the trip is overnight or long enough that you need to sleep or rest to properly perform your duties. For meals, only 50 % of the expense is deductible. Lodging is fully deductible. These limits are outlined in the “Meals and lodging” section 【Segment 1】.  

* **Other incidental expenses** – Deductible items also include cleaning, telephone calls, and tips paid while traveling for business.  

So, to sum up: **yes, you can deduct business travel expenses, but only the portion that is directly related to the business, with specific limits on meals (50 %) and the choice between actual car expenses or the standard mileage rate.**

runs.question: what goes in an executive summary
runs.answer:
An executive summary is the short, two‑paragraph (usually one or two) opening section of a business plan that gives the reader a quick snapshot of the venture. According to the guide, it should:

* Briefly describe your business idea.  
* State how much money you need, what the money will be used for, and how much capital you already have or will contribute.  
* Include a short, high‑level schedule of your goals and milestones.  

The summary is written last because some details are only known after the rest of the plan is finished.  It serves as the “first impression” and lets investors, lenders, or readers know what you want to accomplish and how you plan to do it.  

[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)



**Sources:**

runs.question: how do i describe my target market
runs.answer:
Describe your target market by following these steps:

1. **Identify the niche** – state who your “best customer” is.  
   *Choose a market segment based on obvious categories such as industry, company size, location, product use, demographics, lifestyle, or benefits sought.* [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

2. **Explain the customer characteristics** – describe the key traits that distinguish this group.  
   *For example, age range, income level, geographic area, buying habits, or specific pain points they face.* [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

3. **Segment the market** – break the overall market into sub‑groups that fit your product or service.  
   *In business markets, you might split by industry or company size; for consumer markets, consider demographics or lifestyle.* [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

4. **Estimate market size and growth** – use available data such as population figures, industry reports, or sales tax information to approximate how many potential customers exist and how fast the segment is growing.  
   *Also estimate what percentage of the total market you expect to capture.* [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

5. **Connect location and needs to the target market** – if your business location serves a particular demographic or economic group, mention that in the plan.  
   *Include information such as traffic counts, income levels, or nearby business activity that supports your target market choice.* [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=15)

6. **Tie marketing tactics to the target market** – explain how your promotional strategies (advertising, personal selling, publicity) are specifically tailored to reach and influence that group. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=15)

Following this structure will give viewers of your business plan a clear, data‑driven picture of who you are selling to and why they are the best fit for your offering.

runs.question: do i have to make my shop wheelchair accessible
runs.answer:
Yes.  
The ADA requires that any business that serves the public **must remove physical “barriers” that are “readily achievable.”** This means you have to make your shop accessible to wheelchair users if the changes can be done with reasonable effort and expense. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6)  

For existing businesses built before 1993 the requirements are somewhat less strict, but the same “readily achievable” standard still applies: you must make needed adjustments whenever they can be done without undue cost or difficulty. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=5)  

In practical terms, you would need to provide an accessible route from the sidewalk to the entrance (at least a 32‑inch opening if a turnstile is removed, [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=13)), ensure the entrance itself is accessible, and meet other basic ADA specifications such as a 36‑inch wide aisle, a 36‑inch clear floor space for counters or shelves, and accessible parking if you provide parking. The specific dimensions and minimum widths are found in the various ADA sections above.  

So, unless your shop is already fully compliant, you are required to make it wheelchair accessible to the extent that the changes are readily achievable.



**Sources:**

runs.question: am i exempt from injury recordkeeping
runs.answer:
You are **not automatically exempt** from OSHA injury‑recordkeeping, but you **may be fully exempt** under two specific circumstances described above:

* An employer is fully exempt if **all of the following are true** –  
  – the employer had **10 or fewer workers** during **every calendar month** of the last calendar year, **and**  
  – the employer is **not in one of the low‑hazard industries** listed in 29 CFR Part 1904, Subpart B, Appendix A.  
  This exemption is set out in 29 CFR 1904.1 and is summarized in the handbook here [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14).

* Even when exempt from recording and reporting, you must still:  
  – report **fatalities, in‑patient hospitalizations, amputations, and eye loss** to OSHA within the required time frames (8 hours for fatalities, 24 hours for hospitalization, amputations, eye loss).  
  – keep any required records for at least five years if you are not exempt. The handbook notes these retention rules in the same section [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14) and is reinforced in Segment 2: “Injury and illness records (OSHA 300, 300A, and 301) are kept at the worksite for at least five years” [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15).

So, if you have **10 or fewer workers** for every month of the past calendar year **and** you are **not in a low‑hazard industry**, you are exempt from recording and reporting work‑related injuries and illnesses. If either condition isn’t met, you must follow the normal OSHA recordkeeping and reporting procedures.



**Sources:**
1. [osha_small_business_handbook.pdf (Page 14)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14)
2. [osha_small_business_handbook.pdf (Page 15)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15)
