runs.question: what do i need to do to keep employees safe and my premises accessible
runs.answer:
To keep your employees safe and your premises accessible, you need a coordinated plan that covers **safety and health policies, daily operations, hazard controls, emergency preparedness, and accessibility requirements**. The handbook provides an integrated checklist you can follow:

---

### 1. Safety & Health Program

- **Create a written safety program** that includes management leadership, worker participation, systematic hazard identification, and regular workplace inspections.  
  *[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=7)[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=9)[[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=10)*  

- **Implement training** so workers know how to identify hazards, report injuries, and use protective equipment.  
  *[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=9)[[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=10)*  

- **Set up a system for reporting incidents** and involve workers in hazard‑control decisions.  
  *[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=9)*  

---

### 2. Daily Operations & Inspections

- **Schedule regular inspections** (at least monthly) with workers present to spot hazards and keep walkways clear.  
  *[[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=78)[[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=79)*  

- **Maintain walkways and work surfaces**: keep them clean, free of spills, with adequate headroom, guardrails where needed, and repair holes promptly.  
  *[[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=78)[[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=73)*  

- **Keep equipment and machinery safe**: maintain cleanliness, provide accessible power‑off switches, guard foot‑operated controls, and follow lock‑out/tag‑out procedures.  
  *[[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=54)*  

---

### 3. Ergonomics & Physical Health

- **Use engineering controls** to reduce musculoskeletal risk (e.g., adjustable workstations, material‑lifting devices).  
  *[[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=22)[[9]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=21)*  

- **Train workers** on safe lifting, reaching, and repetitive‑motion practices, and involve them in evaluating controls.  
  *[[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=22)[[9]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=21)*  

- **Provide appropriate PPE** (e.g., head protection near falling objects).  
  *[[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=73)*  

---

### 4. Emergency Preparedness

- **Develop an emergency action plan** that identifies evacuation routes, roles, and assembly points; include procedures for those with disabilities or language barriers.  
  *[[10]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=26)[[11]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=27)*  

- **Mark exits clearly** with illuminated “EXIT” signs (≥6 inches tall, ¾‑inch wide lettering) and ensure exit doors are operable without keys or special effort.  
  *[[12]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=28)[[13]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=23)*  

- **Install and maintain emergency lighting** (test 30 s monthly, 90 min yearly).  
  *[[12]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=28)*  

---

### 5. Accessibility Requirements

| Feature | Key Requirement | Segment |
|---------|----------------|---------|
| **Accessible entrance** | At least one accessible path that is not more than 1:12 slope, with handrails >6 in. if slope >1:20; unlockable or provide a buzzer/ bell at ≤48 in. | 1 |
| **Alternative entrance** | If the accessible entrance cannot be unlocked for security, provide a 32‑in. wide opening or an accessible gate. | 18 |
| **Signage** | Display an international accessibility symbol and “van‑accessible” signs at each accessible space, mounted so they are visible. | 11, 31 |
| **Ramps** | Maximum 1:12 slope, width at least 36 in.; if a ramp is not feasible, consider a lift or platform. | 30 |
| **Parking** | Provide a full‑accessible vehicle space (5 ft. access aisle) and a van‑accessible space if ≥8 total spaces; mount an accessibility symbol. | 31 |
| **Sales / service counters** | Minimum 30×48 in. clear floor space in front of each counters, 36 in. wide access aisle for checkout aisles, and accessible counter height ≤34 in. (38 in. for checkout). | 16 |
| **Seating / tables** | Accessible tables have 28–34 in. height, 27 in. knee clearance, and a 30×48 in. clear floor space. | 24 |
| **Doors** | Accessible doors require lever or loop handles and, where turning space is narrow, provide a 32‑in. opening for wheelchairs. | 36 |
| **Interior aisles / media** | Provide at least 36 in. wide accessible routes, 60‑in. turn‑spaces, or 36‑in. “T” turns. | 22 |

---

### 6. Ongoing Compliance & Resources

- **Document everything**: keep inspection logs, training records, incident reports, and emergency plan reviews.  
  *[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=9)[[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=10)*  

- **Seek assistance** if needed: OSHA On‑Site Consultation programs provide free, confidential help.  
  *[[14]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=90)*  

- **Review applicable OSHA standards** (e.g., 29 CFR 1910.22 for walking‑working surfaces, 1910.23 for stairways, 1910.37 for exit routes).  
  *[[12]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=28)[[15]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=91)*  

---

**Bottom line**:  
1. Build and maintain a written safety program with regular inspections and training.  
2. Keep all walkways, equipment, and work areas clear, properly lit, and compliant with fall‑protection and emergency‑exit standards.  
3. Implement ergonomics best practices to reduce injury risk.  
4. Develop an emergency action plan that includes clear evacuation routes and accommodations for disabled employees.  
5. Ensure the building itself is accessible: provide a fully functional accessible entrance, ramps or lifts, proper signage, clear parking and aisles, and accessible service counters and seating.

Follow the checklists in the handbook and cite the corresponding segments above to verify each requirement is met.

runs.question: how do i write a business plan and set up accounting
runs.answer:
**Writing a Business Plan**

1. **Outline Your Plan** – A recommended structure is given in the guide.  It includes:  
   - Cover page (company name, address, owners, phone, logo, date) – [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)  
   - Table of contents (optional) – [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)  
   - Executive Summary (brief overview, mission, funds needed, schedule of goals) – [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)  
   - Description of the business, products/services, market analysis, competitive advantage, and goals – [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=12)  
   - Marketing strategy and distribution – [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=12)  
   - Management team and personnel details – [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=13)  
   - Financial section (Money) with historical statements, projections, and startup costs – [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=16)  
   - Projections: 3‑year income statement, cash‑flow statement and balance sheet – [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=16)  
   - Sources & Uses of Funds, assumptions, and notes to the pro‑forma – [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=21)  

2. **Fill in Each Section** –  
   - *Executive Summary*: One‑two paragraphs summarizing the plan; write it last once facts are known. – [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)  
   - *Products/Services*: Describe purpose, uniqueness, development stage, suppliers, and quality procedures – [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=12)  
   - *Financial Needs*: Total cost of project, working capital, equity invested, and correlation to the sources‑and‑uses sheet – [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=16)  
   - *Projections*: Monthly forecasts for revenue, cost of goods, expenses and cash flow over three years; back them by market research – [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=16)  
   - *Additional attachments*: Credit reports, leases, contracts, and supporting documents – [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=17)  

**Setting Up Accounting**

1. **Open a Business Checking Account** – Separate from personal funds; deposit all receipts and record in the business checkbook.  Use a checkbook that allows indication of deposit source (income, personal funds, loan).  Reconcile daily – [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=14)

2. **Choose an Accounting Method** –  
   - Cash, Accrual, Special, or Combination – choose when you file your first income tax return and keep it consistent.  A change usually requires IRS approval – [[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)[[9]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=2)[[10]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)  
   - For most small businesses a cash method is allowed; if you hold inventory you may need accrual for inventory – [[10]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)[[11]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16)

3. **Decide on Bookkeeping** –  
   - **Single‑entry**: tracks income‑and‑expense flow with daily and monthly summaries – [[12]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=15)  
   - **Double‑entry**: uses journals and ledgers, recording each transaction as a debit and a credit – [[12]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=15)  
   - Keep separate journals/ledgers for each type of frequent transaction (e.g., sales, payroll, inventory) – [[13]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=13)  

4. **Maintain Detailed Records** –  
   - Record every transaction on the support document (check, receipt, credit‑card slip, bank statement) – [[13]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=13)  
   - Keep a daily summary of cash receipts and a monthly summary of cash receipts and disbursements – [[13]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=13)  
   - Separate business and personal expenses; never write personal checks from the business account – [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=14)  
   - Store records in hard copy and electronically, preserving legible, indexed, recoverable copies for IRS inspection – [[14]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)  

5. **Complete Year‑End Activities** –  
   - Reconcile the bank statement with the checkbook and books – [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=14)  
   - Produce the required tax forms: Schedule C (Form 1040) for income, Schedule SE for self‑employment tax, and any required information returns (W‑2, 1099, etc.) – [[15]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6)  
   - If you have multiple businesses, maintain separate books and filings for each – [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=13)

6. **Other Practical Steps** –  
   - Obtain an Employer Identification Number (EIN) if you have employees or choose to separate your personal SSN – [[16]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=6)  
   - Keep a “checklist” of required documents and deadlines, such as the tax calendar, business licenses, and insurance – [[15]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6)  

By following the outlined structure for your business plan and the record‑keeping, accounting‑method, and bookkeeping procedures described above, you can create a comprehensive plan and maintain accurate, IRS‑acceptable financial records for your new business.



**Sources:**

runs.question: what should i track for taxes and for travel expenses
runs.answer:
**What to track for tax‑related expenses**

| Item to track | Why it matters | Segment source |
|---------------|----------------|----------------|
| **Gross receipts (income)** – amount, source, date | Needed to report income and to determine taxable profit | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12) |
| **Receipts / invoices for every business purchase** – including canceled checks, bank deposit slips, credit‑card slips | Supports entries in books and the tax return; proves the expense was ordinary and necessary | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12) |
| **Bank statements and checkbook records** – shows money paid from the business account | Helps verify that expenses were business‑related and not personal | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11) |
| **Payroll documents** – employee hours, wages, withholdings | Required for payroll tax returns and to calculate moments of deduction | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11) |
| **Inventory records** – purchase, sale, ending balance | Required for C‑form Schedule C Part III (inventory) and for depreciation | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12) |
| **Depreciation schedules** – for property, machinery, furniture | Needed to claim the yearly deduction on Schedule C | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11) |
| **Tax payment records** – estimated tax payments, filing dates, vouchers | Needed to prove you paid tax on time and to avoid penalties | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11) |
| **Vehicle log books (if using car/truck)** – miles driven for business, commuting, personal | Determines percentage of deductible vehicle costs | [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=36) |
| **Travel logs** – destination, purpose, dates, mileage, lodging, meals, tips, transportation | Needed to separate business from personal travel, calculate mileage or actual expense deductions | [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=13)[[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41)[[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=35) |

**What to track for travel expenses (business trips)**  

| Travel expense type | How to track it | Segment source |
|---------------------|----------------|----------------|
| **Mileage** – number of miles driven *for business* | Record start and end odometer, purpose of each trip | [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=36) |
| **Tolls, parking fees, parking minimums** | Keep receipts or entry logs | [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=35) |
| **Airs, trains, rideshare fares** | Keep original receipts / transport booking confirmation | [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=35) |
| **Lodging (hotel, Airbnb, etc.)** | Keep invoice/receipt and note business purpose | [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41) |
| **Meals** – cost, date, location, business purpose | Keep receipts; note business relationship of diners | [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41) |
| **Tips** – for hotel, taxi, dinner service | Keep receipts or manually record amount | [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41) |
| **Business phone/communication** – calls, fax, text | Keep logs or receipts showing business use | [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41) |
| **Other travel items** – dry‑cleaning, laundry, transportation to temporary workplaces | Keep receipts; note business purpose | [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41) |
| **Day‑trip vs. overnight** – identify if trip requires sleep/rest | Only overnight or “long enough” trips are deductible | [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40) |

**Key rules that influence what you **can** deduct**

- You may deduct **50 % of meal expenses** (unless the meal is a “qualified” business meal, then 100 %) [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41).
- The **standard mileage rate** or actual costs can be used for vehicle expenses; keep a mileage log if you use the mileage rate [[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=34).
- **Travel away from home** is deductible only if your duties require you to be *away from the general area of your tax home for longer than an ordinary day’s work* *and* you need sleep or rest [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40).
- **Local transportation** (from one workplace to another within the tax‑home area) is deductible as a local transportation expense [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=35).
- The **reimbursement** of employees for travel and meal expenses is deductible, but how it is reported depends on whether the plan is accountable or non‑accountable (see Pub. 15) [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41).
- When you **cash in** receipts for larger payments, attach a petty‑cash slip and receipt as proof [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=13).

**Bottom line**

For taxes you need a complete file of income and expense evidence: receipts, invoices, canceled checks, bank statements, payroll records, and depreciation schedules.  
For business travel you keep a log of mileage, lodging, meals, tips, transportation, and other related expenses, together with receipts that show the business purpose.  All these records support the deductions you claim on your tax return and defend you in case of an IRS inquiry.

runs.question: do i need an ein and what accounting method comes with it
runs.answer:
Yes, you will usually need an EIN (Employer Identification Number) if your business is more than just a lump‑sum, sole‑proprietor operation that never hires anyone. An EIN is required  

* if you pay wages to employees,  
* if you file pension or excise‑tax returns, or  
* if you simply want a separate tax ID for your business instead of using your personal Social Security number.  
These rules are laid out in the IRS guidance: [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=4) and [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6).

The EIN itself does **not** dictate a particular accounting method. When you file your first income‑tax return you choose either the cash or accrual method (or a special combination that still shows your income). That decision is made the same way whether you file with an EIN or just an SSN:  

* Cash method – report income when you receive it, expenses when you pay them.  
* Accrual method – report income when it is earned, expenses when they are incurred.  
(See the discussion of accounting methods in [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5) and the extended guidance in [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=28) and [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15).)

So:

| Question | Answer |
|----------|--------|
| Do I need an EIN? | Yes, if you meet any of the conditions outlined above (e.g., have employees or file specific federal tax returns). |
| What accounting method comes with an EIN? | No specific method is tied to an EIN; you choose either cash or accrual (or a combination that follows IRS rules) when you file your first return. |

If you are a sole proprietor without employees and have no other reason to obtain an EIN, you may use your SSN for tax reporting, but obtaining an EIN is often simpler for future business transactions.

runs.question: what forms do i keep for injuries and how long do i keep them
runs.answer:
For work‑related injuries you must keep the OSHA‑required records:  

* **OSHA Form 300** – the Log of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses, for every recordable injury or illness (minor first‑aid cases need not be logged). [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14)

These forms must be retained at the worksite for **at least five (5) years** after the date they are created or after the injury/illness event, whichever is later. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15)

runs.question: do i need workers comp insurance and can i deduct it
runs.answer:
Yes, most states require a business that has employees to carry workers’‑compensation insurance. The law requires coverage for any claims for bodily injury or job‑related disease that an employee experiences.  

Because the insurance is “set by state law” it is a normal and necessary business expense, and the Internal Revenue Service lets you deduct the premiums you pay on Schedule C.  
[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=37)  

If you do choose to carry the coverage, the premium expense can be deducted as a business expense on the appropriate tax return. No additional deduction rules beyond the ordinary deductible business‑expense rules are needed.  
[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=37)

runs.question: what do i file for my employees and what state taxes do i owe for them
runs.answer:
For each person you employ you must report and pay a set of federal and state payroll taxes.  The IRS requires the following filings for every employee:  

1. **W‑2, Wage and Tax Statement** – Reports wages, tips, other compensation, withholding for federal income tax, Social Security and Medicare taxes, and (if applicable) state income tax.  File each year and also file a transmittal **W‑3** that summarizes all the W‑2s you submit.  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=9)  
2. **W‑4, Employee’s Withholding Allowance Certificate** – Employees submit this so you can withhold the correct amount of federal income tax.  The employer must keep the W‑4 on file.  [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=7)  
3. **Form I‑9, Employment Eligibility Verification** – Confirms each employee’s right to work in the United States.  Keep the completed I‑9 for each new hire.  [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=7)  
4. **Form 941, Employer’s QUARTERLY Federal Tax Return** (or **Form 944, Employer’s ANNUAL Federal Tax Return** if your liability is small) – Reports the total wages paid and the amounts of Social Security and Medicare taxes you withhold and pay, plus federal income tax withheld.  [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=7)  
5. **Form 940, Employer’s Annual Federal Unemployment (FUTA) Tax Return** – Reports the federal unemployment tax you owe (paid only by the employer; not withheld from employees).  [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=7)

**State‑level obligations**

- **State unemployment insurance contributions** – Every employer must make quarterly contributions to the state’s unemployment insurance fund.  The amount and due dates are set by the state.  Contact the state’s Department of Labor for specific rates and filing procedures.  [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=9)  
- Many states also require employers to withhold state income tax and to file state payroll‑tax returns (the specific form and due date depend on the state).  While the segment text does not list every state form, the requirement to pay state unemployment insurance and to withhold state income tax is implied by the state’s unemployment‑insurance filing requirement.  [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=9)

**Summary of what you file**

| Federal/State Form | Purpose | When to File | Source |
|--------------------|---------|--------------|--------|
| W‑2 | Employee wage & tax summary | Next year’s January (or later) | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=9) |
| W‑3 | Transmittal of W‑2s | Same as W‑2 | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=9) |
| W‑4 | Employee withholding

runs.question: what if a customer cannot get through my front door and what if someone is hurt on site
runs.answer:
The context segments do answer both parts of your question.  

**1. A customer can’t get through the front door**  
- If the main entrance is not accessible, you must provide an alternative entrance that is accessible and keep it open during business hours. Signage has to direct people to that entrance.  
  – “When one entrance is not accessible and another entrance is accessible, **a sign must provide direction to the accessible entrance**” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10).  
  – The alternative entrance must be open during store hours [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10).  
- If the door itself is a barrier, first‑step modifications can make it usable.  
  – “A door that is less than 36 in. wide … may be enlarged … or a lever handle can be added or a round knob replaced” [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=12).  
  – Adding a ramp, handrails and a wide landing, with edge protection, can give a wheelchair‑friendly entrance (“Edge protection … prevents people from accidentally rolling off the edge of the ramp.”) [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=11).  
- If a turnstile or security gate blocks entry, it can be removed or replaced with an accessible gate, or a second entrance can be used.  
  – “If an inaccessible turnstile is located at the entrance … it must be replaced or removed or an alternate accessible entrance provided” [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=13).  

**2. Someone is hurt on site**  
- First, provide immediate first aid and medical care. If the injury is minor and requires only first aid, OSHA record‑keeping rules say it is not required.  
- If the injury is recordable, you must:  
  – Log it on OSHA Form 300 (Log of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses).  
  – Complete Form 301 (Injury and Illness Incident Report) and keep a supplementary record.  
  – At year‑end prepare Form 300A (Summary of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses).  
  – Employers who had 10 or fewer workers or work in a low‑hazard industry may be partly exempt, but still must report fatalities, hospitalizations, amputations, and eye loss to OSHA.  
  – “Occupational injuries or illnesses … are recorded on OSHA Form 300” [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14).  
- Maintain a workplace safety program that includes incident reporting and a written plan for violence prevention and general safety.  
  – “A written program is in place to prevent workplace violence … the program is reviewed annually” [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=85).  

These segments together give you the specific actions you need to take for accessibility and for handling injuries on your premises.

runs.question: why should i bother with a safety program and what records do i need to keep
runs.answer:
Because a safety program is a way to protect the people who work for you and to keep your business running smoothly.

**Why bother with a safety program?**  
* It stops injuries, illnesses and deaths before they happen, so you avoid the loss of workers, the cost of workers‑compensation claims, and the possible legal penalties that come with accidents [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=6).  
* A program shows that you care about employees, boosts morale, and can save money in the long run by cutting lost‑time days, insurance premiums, and equipment damage [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=7).  
* OSHA encourages all workplaces to have one (the “Safe + Sound” campaign) and many states require it for certain industries [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=6)[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=7).

**What records do you need to keep?**  
| Record | What it is | How long to keep it | Key points |
|--------|-----------|---------------------|------------|
| **OSHA Form 300 – Log of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses** | Daily log of any injury or illness that requires first aid, medical treatment, or results in lost work time [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14) | At least **5 years** [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) | Keep at the worksite; must be available for inspection by workers and OSHA. |
| **OSHA Form 301 – Injury and Illness Incident Report** | Supplemental details for each recordable case [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14) | Same as Form 300 [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) | Use the OSHA form or an equivalent form that has the same information. |
| **OSHA Form 300A – Summary of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses** | Annual summary of the year’s log and incident reports [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14) | Same as Forms 300/301 [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) | File electronically if you have ≥ 100 workers in a high‑hazard industry (submit by March 2 of the following year) [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15). |
| **Medical and exposure records** | Workers’ health data, such as lost‑time conditions or exposure to hazardous substances [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) | Retain for the period required by the specific type of record (often the statutory length) [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) | Must be accessible to employees under 29 CFR 1910.1020. |
| **Training records** | Documentation that workers were trained on how to identify and control hazards [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) | Keep them so workers can review them when needed [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) | OSHA requires that training records be available for worker review. |
| **Fatality and severe‑injury reports** | Must be filed immediately to OSHA [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) | - | Report any work‑related fatality within **8 hours**; hospitalizations, amputations, or eye loss within **24 hours** (also report to workers’ comp). |
| **Other record‑keeping/maintenance records** | Equipment maintenance logs, inspection reports, hazard assessments, and any incident‑report forms you use in place of OSHA forms [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14) | Keep as long as you need to support the record‑keeping and reporting rules [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) | Keeps you ready for an OSHA inspection or audit. |

### Quick checklist  
1. **Log every recordable injury/illness** on Form 300.  
2. **Provide a detailed incident report** on Form 301.  
3. **Prepare the yearly summary** with Form 300A.  
4. **Keep all logs, reports, training records, and medical data** for at least five years.  
5. **Report any fatality or severe injury** to OSHA right away.  

By keeping these records, you meet OSHA’s legal requirements, protect your workers, and reduce the financial risks to your business.

runs.question: how do i register a trademark
runs.answer:
The context that actually explains how to register a trademark is found in **Segment 1**. It tells you that trademarks can be registered either at the state level or the federal level, and gives the main contact points for each option. No other segment in the provided text gives a step‑by‑step registration procedure or additional deadlines.

**How to register a trademark**

1. **Decide where to register**  
   – You can register the mark with your state’s Secretary of State office **or** with the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO) for a federal registration.  

2. **Search the database**  
   – Before filing, search the applicable trademark databases (state or USPTO’s TESS system) to ensure your chosen name or mark has not already been registered.  

3. **File the application**  
   – For a state registration, file the form required by your state’s Secretary of State office.  
   – For a federal registration, file the application online through the USPTO’s website.

4. **Pay the fees**  
   – Each jurisdiction has its own fee schedule; be sure to follow the instructions on the Secretary of State site or the USPTO site.

5. **Track the status**  
   – After filing, you can monitor the status of your application through the same government portal you used to file.

**Contact information**

- **State level:** Secretary of State – (605) 773‑2797, website: [sdsos.gov](https://sdsos.gov/) [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=10)  
- **Federal level:** U.S. Patent and Trademark Office – (703) 308‑HELP or (800) 786‑9199, website: [www.uspto.gov](http://www.uspto.gov) [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=10)

runs.question: how long do i keep tax records
runs.answer:
You must keep your tax‑related records for the time periods that the IRS says are required:

* **General tax returns** – Keep any books, documents, or other records that support an item of income or deduction on a tax return **until the period of limitations for that return expires**. The periods of limitations for different returns are listed in IRS Table 3 (see Section 1). Keep a copy of each filed return for the same period.  
  *[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)*  

* **Employment‑tax records** – If you have employees, retain all employment‑tax records for **at least 4 years after the tax becomes due or is paid, whichever is later**.  
  *[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)*  

* **Asset‑related records** – Keep records that describe any property you own (purchase price, improvements, depreciation, etc.) **until the period of limitations expires for the year you dispose of that property in a taxable disposition**. This is the time needed to determine basis and calculate gain or loss.  
  *[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)*  

In short, keep records as long as the IRS might need them for determining tax liability or for an audit—generally the period of limitations for the specific return, plus 4 years for employment taxes, and until the limitation period expires for the year you sell or dispose of property.



**Sources:**
1. [irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf (Page 16)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)

runs.question: why do i need to keep business records
runs.answer:
You need to keep business records for several practical and legal reasons:

* **Track how the business is doing** – Accurate records let you see whether sales are growing, which products sell best, and which changes may be needed. This helps you make better decisions and can improve the chance of success. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)  
* **Prepare financial statements** – Income‑statement and balance‑sheet reports are built from the underlying records. These statements are needed to manage the business and to show banks or creditors how you’re performing. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)  
* **Identify the source of receipts** – Records tell you where money and property came from, so you can separate business income from personal receipts and distinguish taxable from non‑taxable amounts. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)  
* **Track deductible expenses** – If you record purchases when they occur, you won’t forget items that can reduce your taxable income when you file your return. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)  
* **Prepare tax returns** – The figures you report on your tax forms must be backed up by supporting records. Keeping those records makes the return accurate and complete. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)  
* **Support tax‑return information** – The IRS can ask for evidence of the numbers on your return. Having a complete set of records ready lets you explain items quickly and can speed up any audit. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)  

In short, keeping thorough records helps you run the business more effectively, shows you how the business is performing, and satisfies tax and regulatory requirements.



**Sources:**

runs.question: how do i check my workplace for hazards
runs.answer:
To check your workplace for hazards, follow the step‑by‑step process outlined in the Small Business Safety and Health Handbook:

1. **Conduct a routine self‑inspection**  
   • Have knowledgeable workers walk the worksite and evaluate each area, process, and piece of equipment directly.  
   • Use the self‑inspection checklists included in the handbook. These checklists are a starting point for identifying workplace hazards in general‑industry settings (but not for construction or maritime) and show you where to begin taking action.  
   – [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)

2. **Compile supporting information**  
   • Combine the completed checklists with injury, illness, and incident records, worker training logs, maintenance logs, and any failure reports.  
   • This compilation helps you spot patterns and determine which hazards need control procedures.  
   – [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)

3. **Review applicable OSHA standards**  
   • Look up the OSHA standards that apply to your business type, equipment, and materials.  
   • If a standard does not cover a hazard you’ve identified, the “general duty clause” may apply.  
   – [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=91)

4. **Seek expert help if needed**  
   • OSHA’s On‑Site Consultation program offers free, confidential help from trained consultants who can guide you through a hazard assessment and recommend controls.  
   • Contact your local state or university‑based program to schedule a visit.  
   – [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=90)

5. **Implement controls and monitor effectiveness**  
   • Once hazards are identified and controls are put in place, periodically re‑inspect to verify that the controls remain effective and adjust as circumstances change.  
   – [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)

By following these steps you’ll systematically identify, evaluate, and control hazards in your workplace.

runs.question: cash or accrual accounting whats the difference
runs.answer:
Cash and accrual accounting differ mainly in **when** a business records its income and expenses.

* **Cash method** – Income is reported the year the money is actually or constructively received, and expenses are deducted the year the cash is paid.  
  * “Under the cash method, include in your gross income all items of income you actually or constructively receive during your tax year.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)  
  * “When you receive a payment in January 2025 for a service performed in December 2024, you must include that amount in 2025 income.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)

* **Accrual method** – Income is reported the year it is earned (when the sale is made or the service is rendered), and expenses are reported the year they are incurred, regardless of cash flow.  
  * “Under an accrual method of accounting, you generally report income in the year earned and deduct or capitalize expenses in the year incurred.” [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15)  
  * Example: “You sold a computer on December 28 2025 but billed the customer in early January 2026 and received payment in February 2026. You must include the amount in 2025 income.” [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15)

**Key differences**

| Aspect | Cash method | Accrual method |
|--------|-------------|----------------|
| Income timing | When cash is received (or made available without restriction) | When the right to receive payment is fixed and the amount can be determined |
| Expense timing | When cash is paid | When the expense is incurred (liability is fixed) |
| Inventory requirement | Not required unless you have inventory | If inventory is necessary to account for your income, you must generally use accrual for purchases and sales | [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16) |

Thus, cash accounting matches money in and money out, while accrual accounting matches the economic event—earning or incurring—regardless of cash flow.



**Sources:**
1. [irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 14)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)
2. [irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 15)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15)

runs.question: can i deduct business travel
runs.answer:
Yes. The IRS allows a business owner to deduct the costs that are directly associated with traveling for business. Here’s what the guidance says:

- **Transportation between home and a business destination** – You can deduct the cost of air, train, bus, or car travel.  
  *[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40)*

- **Local transportation at the destination** – Fares for taxis, commuter buses, limousines, or other local travel (between the airport/station and your hotel, or between the hotel and the work site) are deductible.  
  *[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40)*

- **Car or truck use while away from home** – You may deduct either (a) actual out‑of‑pocket expenses such as fuel, repair, tolls, and parking, or (b) the IRS’s standard mileage rate (70 ¢ per mile for 2025). If you rent a car, you can deduct only the portion that is for business.  
  *[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40)[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)*

- **Baggage and shipping** – The cost of sending baggage, samples, or display material between your usual and temporary work locations is deductible.  
  *[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40)*

- **Meals and lodging** – If the trip is overnight or long enough that you must sleep or rest to perform your work, you can deduct lodging in full. For meals you can deduct either the actual expense (up to 50 % of the cost) or the standard meal allowance.  
  *[[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41)*

- **Other incidental expenses** – Cleaning, telephone calls, and tips that are linked to the travel can also be deducted.  
  *[[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41)*

- **Reimbursement to employees** – If you reimburse employees for travel and meal costs, those reimbursements are generally deductible, but how you report them depends on whether you use an accountable or non‑accountable plan.  
  *[[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41)*

So, in short, business travel expenses—including transport to and from the destination, local trips, car use, baggage, meals (50 % deductible), lodging, and other incidental costs—are deductible provided they are ordinary and necessary for your business.



**Sources:**
1. [irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 40)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40)

runs.question: how do i describe my target market
runs.answer:
To describe your target market, follow the structure below:

1. **Define the niche** – “Describe your market niche; who is your best customer.” Identify the specific group of people or businesses that will benefit most from what you offer.  
2. **Identify characteristics** – For business markets, segment by industry, company size, location, or product use/application. For consumer markets, segment by demographics (age, gender), geographic location, economic status, lifestyle, product application, or benefits sought.  
3. **Estimate size and growth** – Use population figures, sales tax data, industry reports, or other statistics to estimate the approximate size of the target market and its growth potential.  
4. **Project market share** – Estimate how much of the total market you expect to capture with your product or service.  

These steps give a clear, data‑driven description of who your customers are and how large the opportunity is.  

[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

runs.question: do i have to make my shop wheelchair accessible
runs.answer:
Yes.  Because your shop serves the public, the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) requires you to remove “readily‑achievable” barriers that prevent people who use wheelchairs from accessing the business.  In practice this means:

| What you must provide | Specified requirement in the ADA | Source |
|------------------------|------------------------------------|--------|
| **Accessible entrance** – at least one public entrance must be usable by a wheelchair, with a clear approach that has no steps or a curb‑cut of at least 36 in.  If the shop has a second entrance, it need **not** be accessible, but you must signpost a direction to the accessible one, and that alternate entrance must stay open during business hours. | “If one entrance is not accessible and another entrance is accessible… a sign must provide direction to the accessible entrance.” | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10) |
| **Ramp or alternative** – if a step or series of steps are unavoidable, you must either provide a ramp (maximum 1:12 slope, 36‑in minimum width) or another means (lift, powered platform, or accessible gate).  The opening must be at least 32 in if a turnstile is removed. | “The ramp slope max. 1:12 and width is 36" minimum … If an inaccessible turnstile is located at the entrance … an alternative accessible entrance … must be provided.” | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=11) |
| **Clearway in front of accessible counters** – a 30‑by‑48‑in. clear floor space for a customer using a wheelchair to pull alongside the counter, connected to the accessible route. | “…clear floor space … 30 in by 48 in … connected to the accessible route…” | [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15) |
| **Accessible sales aisles** – provide a minimum of a 36‑in wide aisle, and any aisle that contains a counter higher than 34 in must have a lowered section no higher than 34 in and at least 60 in long. | “Checkout aisles … minimum of a 36‑inch‑wide access aisle… counter adjacent … maximum height 38 in… if a lip is provided… 40 in.” | [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15) |
| **Accessible shelving / merchandise** – maintain a 36‑in wide accessible route around shelves, with a 3‑by‑3‑ft turning space at corners and a 60‑in diameter “T” turn if needed. | “…Provide at least a 3' by 3' turning space… 36‑in wide accessible route… 60‑in diameter turning space or a 36‑in wide “T”.” | [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14) |
| **Accessible serving counter** – if the counter is >34 in high, provide a lowered section that is no higher than 34 in and at least 60 in long, or provide service at an adjacent accessible table. | “Where food or drinks are served at counters… providing a lowered section… at least 60 in long and no higher than 34 in.” | [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16) |
| **Accessible parking** – if you have a parking lot, furnish at least one accessible parking space (or two if you have 51–75 spaces, etc.) with a 5‑ft wide access aisle (or 8‑ft for vans). The space must be as near as possible to the accessible entrance, on level ground, with a clear vertical clearance of 98 in. | “An accessible parking space … 5'-0" min. … 8'-0" min. … Accessible parking spaces should be the spaces closest to the accessible entrance.” | [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=8) |
| **Barrier removal priority** – when you can’t make a feature fully accessible, you can provide an alternative service or accessible location for the same goods/services, as long as it is “readily achievable.” | “If it is not readily achievable to provide … the goods and services must be provided in some other way, if doing so is readily achievable.” | [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6) |
| **Signage** – place a sign with the international accessibility symbol over any accessible route or entrance, and place a sign with the symbol over each accessible parking space. | “…a sign with the international symbol of accessibility must be located in front of the parking space… sign with the international symbol of accessibility mounted….” | [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=8) |
| **Policies & procedures** – if you have a policy that denies service or restricts seating to one area, you must revise it so people in wheelchairs have the same choices as others. | “…the policy should be changed to permit people who use service animals… the policy to permit the range of choices enjoyed by others.” | [[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=18) |

**Bottom line**  
Any barrier that can be removed without undue expense or effort must be removed.  If a full modification (e.g., a ramp or lowered counter) is not “readily achievable,” you may provide an alternative service or entrance, but the store must still be accessible whenever possible.  If you provide parking, a minimum number of accessible spots must be offered.  When in doubt, consult the ADA’s “Technical Assistance” resources listed on the DOJ

runs.question: how long do i have to report a workplace death
runs.answer:
You must report a work‑related fatality to OSHA within **8 hours** of learning of the death.  

This requirement is stated in the recordkeeping and reporting sections of the handbook: “All work‑related fatalities are reported to OSHA within 8 hours.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) and repeated in the infection‑control section: “work‑related infectious diseases resulting in a fatality are reported to OSHA within 8 hours.” [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=48)

runs.question: when do i report an amputation to osha
runs.answer:
You must report an amputation to OSHA within **24 hours** of the incident. If the injury is a fatality, the report must be made within **8 hours**. This requirement is set out for all work‑related inpatient hospitalizations, amputations, and loss of an eye in OSHA’s reporting rules [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15).

runs.question: am i exempt from injury recordkeeping
runs.answer:
You can be exempt from OSHA’s injury‑recordkeeping if you meet one of the following conditions listed in the handbook:

- You had **10 or fewer workers** during every month of the last calendar year, **or**
- Your business is in a **low‑hazard industry** specified in 29 CFR Part 1904, Subpart B, Appendix A.  

All employers, regardless of size or industry, must still record and report work‑related **fatalities, in‑patient hospitalizations, amputations, and loss of an eye** to OSHA [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14).

runs.question: what records do i keep for tax and for injuries and for how long
runs.answer:
**Tax records**

* Keep any documents that support the income, deductions, or credits you report on a tax return until the period of limitations for that return expires.  
  * “You must keep your records … until the period of limitations for that return runs out.”  
  * “Keep copies of your filed tax returns.” – [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)  
* If you have employees, keep all employment‑tax records for **at least 4 years** after the tax becomes due or is paid (whichever is later).  
  * “If you have employees, you must keep all employment tax records for at least 4 years after the date the tax becomes due or is paid …” – [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)  
* Keep records relating to property (assets) until the period of limitations expires for the year in which you dispose of the property.  
  * “Keep records relating to property until the period of limitations expires for the year in which you dispose of the property….” – [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)  

**Injury (OSHA) records**

* Record every occupational injury or illness on OSHA Form 300 (the Log of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses).  
  * “Occupational injuries or illnesses... are recorded on OSHA Form 300.” – [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15)  
* For recordable cases, keep a supplementary record on OSHA Form 301 (Injury and Illness Incident Report).  
  * “A supplementary record of each recordable occupational injury and illness is prepared for recordable cases on OSHA Form 301.” – [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15)  
* At the end of each calendar year prepare OSHA Form 300A (Summary of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses).  
  * “An annual summary is prepared at the end of each calendar year using OSHA Form 300A.” – [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15)  
* Retain all injury and illness records (Forms 300, 300A, and 301) **for at least five years** at the worksite.  
  * “Injury and illness records (OSHA 300, 300A, and 301) are kept at the worksite for at least five years.” – [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15)  
* Keep worker medical and exposure records for the time period required for each specific type of record; keep training records accessible as required by OSHA.  
  * “Worker medical and exposure records are retained for the time period required for each specific type of record.” – [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15)  

**Summary**

- **Tax:** keep supporting documentation for the life of the applicable period of limitations, retain copies of filed returns, keep employment‑tax records **≥ 4 years**, and preserve asset records until the period of limitations on the year of disposal.  
- **Injury:** keep OSHA Forms 300, 300A, 301 and related records for **≥ 5 years**, plus any medical or training records required by OSHA for the prescribed durations.

runs.question: how do i start a business and keep my taxes organized
runs.answer:
**How to start a business and keep your taxes organized**

---

## 1.  Decide the legal form of the business  

| Step | What you need to know | Where it’s found |
|------|-----------------------|------------------|
| Choose a structure (sole proprietorship, partnership, LLC, corporation, etc.) | Determines ownership, liability, and the tax return you must file | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=2) |
| FILE for a name (fictitious, assumed) if you’re not using a personal name | Register with county or state secretary of state | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=6) |
| Get an EIN if you will hire employees, pay excise tax, or simply want a business tax ID | Apply via IRS Form SS‑4 | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=6) |

> “If you have employees or pay Federal Excise Tax, a Federal Employer's Identification Number (EIN) must be obtained from Internal Revenue Service.” [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=6)  

---

## 2.  Pick a tax year and accounting method  

| Decision | Key point | Source |
|----------|-----------|--------|
| Tax year | Either a calendar year (Jan 1 – Dec 31) or a fiscal year ending any month except December | [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14) |
| Automatic change | You may change to a fiscal year by filing Form 1128 ; a fee may be waived if you qualify | [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14) |
| Accounting method | Cash or accrual; use the method that clearly shows income and expenses for the tax year | [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12) |

> “You must use an accounting method that clearly shows your income and expenses for the tax year.” [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)  

---

## 3.  Set up a bookkeeping system  

| What to keep | Why it matters | Source |
|---------------|-----------------|--------|
| Register of income and expenses (cash book, ledger, bank statements) | These records are needed to prepare financial statements, tax returns and to support deductions | [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11) |
| Separate books per business if you own more than one | Keeps deductions and income distinct | [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12) |
| Electronic storage must be full‑scale (index, preserve, reproduce) | IRS will have the same rights to your electronic records as to paper ones | [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12) |

> “Good records can increase the likelihood of business success.” [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)  

---

## 4.  Know which taxes you owe and how to report/pay them  

| Type of tax | Who pays it | How to file/pay | Key details |
|-------------|-------------|-----------------|-------------|
| **Income tax** | All businesses (corporations, LLCs, sole proprietors) | Schedule C (or G, L, etc.) with Form 1040; or Form 1120 for corporations | “All businesses except partnerships must file an annual income tax return.” [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5) |
| **Self‑employment tax** | Sole proprietors, partners, S‑corp shareholders | Schedule SE (Form 1040) | “Self‑employment tax is on Schedule SE.” [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=47) |
| **Employment taxes** | Employers | Forms 940 (FUTA), 941/942 (social‑security & Medicare), W‑2, W‑3, 1099‑NEC/MISC | “Provide Forms W‑2…” [[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=13); “You must file Forms 1099‑NEC…and 1099‑MISC if paid ≥$600.”  |
| **Estimated tax** | Anyone who expects to owe $1,000+ in income tax or a corporation $500+ | Form 1040‑ES (individual), a corporate estimated‑tax schedule | “If you expect to owe $1,000 or more…use Form 1040‑ES.” [[9]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=6) |
| **Excise taxes** | Applicable to specific products or activities | Forms specific to the excise tax (e.g., 634 for commercial fuel) | “You may have to file forms to report employment taxes, excise taxes, etc.” [[10]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=8) |
| **Other filings** | Business close‑outs, name changes | Form W‑3, 1096 for information returns | “Table 1‑3” [[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=13) |

**Due dates**  
- Form 940 (FUTA) is filed annually; the due date is the last day of the month following the quarter, e.g., December 31 for the final quarter.  
- Forms 941/942 are filed quarterly (April 30, July 31, October 31, January 31).  
- Form 1040‑ES payments are due April 15, June 15, September 15, and January 15 of the following year.  
- Information‑return forms (W‑2, 1099‑NEC/MISC) must be filed with the IRS by January 31; copies must be mailed to recipients by February 28 (or March 31 if e‑filing).  

> “File Form 940… for the calendar year in which final wages were paid.” [[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=13)  
> “Provide Form W‑2 to your employees… File Form 1096 to file…Forms 1099‑MISC and 1099‑NEC.” [[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=13)  
> “File Form 1040‑ES… if you expect to owe tax of $1,000 or more.” [[9]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=6)  

---

## 5.  Deductible business expenses  

| Category | How it’s treated | Key limits | Source |
|---------|-----------------|------------|--------|
| Start‑up and organizational costs | Can write off up to $5,000 each, reduced by amounts over $50,000 | $5,000 each | “You can elect to deduct up to $5
