runs.question: what do i file for my employees and what state taxes do i owe for them
runs.answer:
You’ll need to file a handful of federal forms that report what you pay your employees and the taxes you withhold, and you’ll also be required to pay state‑level payroll taxes (at least the state unemployment fund and, in most states, state income‑tax withholding).  The context below gives the specific federal forms you must file and the state‑level tax that is mentioned.

| What you file | Why you file | Reference |
|--------------|--------------|-----------|
| **Form W‑2** – Wage and Tax Statement | Reports each employee’s wages, tips, withheld federal income tax, Social Security and Medicare taxes, and the amounts you pay on their behalf.  Employers must give a copy to the employee and file a copy with the Social Security Administration. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=9) |
| **Form W‑3** – Transmittal of Forms W‑2 | A summary of all W‑2s you file for the year. | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=13) |
| **Form 941** – Employer’s QUARTERLY Federal Tax Return (or **Form 944** – ANNUAL) | Reports quarterly amounts withheld for federal income tax, Social Security and Medicare taxes, and your employer’s share of those payroll taxes. | [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=7) |
| **Form 940** – Employer’s Annual Federal Unemployment (FUTA) Tax Return | Reports the federal unemployment tax you pay (no employee share). | [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=7) |
| **Form I‑9** | Verifies that each employee is legally eligible to work in the U.S.; required before you can withhold taxes. | [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=7) |
| **Form W‑4** | Employee completes this so you can compute the correct amount of federal income tax to withhold. | [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=7) |

### State‑level payroll taxes

* **State Unemployment Insurance (SUI) tax** – Employers must make quarterly contributions to the state’s unemployment insurance fund.  For example, in South Dakota the employer contributes to the **State Unemployment Tax** and you can find the department contact and required reporting windows in the state labor office.  The contribution rate and due dates are set by the state; the employer is the sole payer. | [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=9) |

> *What’s missing:* The segments do not provide the exact rates or due dates for other state taxes such as state income‑tax withholding, state disability insurance, or other state‑specific payroll taxes. You’ll need to check your state’s labor or revenue department for those details.

**Bottom line**  
- File **W‑2/W‑3**, **941** or **944**, **940**, **I‑9** and **W‑4** for each employee.  
- Pay the state unemployment tax (and any other state‑specific payroll taxes that apply).  
- For details on rates, deadlines, and any additional state filing requirements, consult the tax department (or the “State Unemployment Tax” guidance in your state’s labor office).

runs.question: what if a customer cannot get through my front door and what if someone is hurt on site
runs.answer:
**If a customer cannot get through my front door**

- The ADA requires that *at least one* entrance be accessible.  If the front door is not accessible, you must provide and keep open an alternate accessible entrance at all business hours.  A clear sign must direct customers to that entrance.  The sign must be visible and readable. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10)  
- If the barrier is a turnstile or other gate, you must either remove it or replace it with an accessible gate that provides at least a 32‑inch opening, or point customers to an existing accessible door. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=13)

**If someone is hurt on site**

- First aid: A fully supplied first‑aid kit must be easily accessible in each work area, and at least one employee on each shift must be trained to give first aid. If the workplace lacks a nearby medical facility, at least one employee must be qualified for first aid, and if the employee’s role includes responding to emergencies, they should have received additional training and hepatitis‑B vaccination. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=62)  
- Emergency action plan: The plan must identify evacuation conditions, a chain of command, evacuation routes, and procedures for assisting people with disabilities or who do not speak English. It must also include procedures for accounting for workers and visitors after evacuation. [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=26)  
- Injury recording: Any injury that requires more than first help must be logged on OSHA Form 300, a detailed incident report on Form 301, and an annual summary on Form 300A.  Employers with 10 or fewer workers may be partially exempt, but still must report fatalities, hospitalizations, amputations, and eye loss. [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14)  
- General safety: Work‐site walking surfaces must be kept clean, free of hazards, and have adequate guardrails for elevated areas.  A good emergency exit network and visible exit signs are also required. [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=79)[[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=78)[[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=28)

These guidelines come directly from the small‑business safety and health handbook and address both parts of the question.

runs.question: why should i bother with a safety program and what records do i need to keep
runs.answer:
People who put a safety program in place usually see **fewer injuries, lower insurance costs, and happier workers**.  OSHA’s own data show that a well‑run program can cut injury rates and keep a business from costly investigations or penalties.  Having a program also helps you **avoid future losses** – inspections are smoother, workers stay healthier, and the business stays “sound” in the long run.  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=6)

### What types of records must you keep?

| Record | What it covers | How long you must keep it | Note |
|--------|----------------|---------------------------|------|
| **OSHA Form 300 (Log of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses)** | Any injury or illness that requires first aid, causes loss of a workday, or meets other criteria | **5 years** at the worksite | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |
| **OSHA Form 301 (Injury and Illness Incident Report)** | Detailed report for each recordable case | **5 years** at the worksite (same as Form 300) | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |
| **OSHA Form 300‑A (Summary of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses)** | Annual summary of the year’s 300/301 data | **5 years** at the worksite | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |
| **Electronic submission to OSHA** | Upload 300/301 data if you’re a 100‑plus‑worker high‑hazard business | Submit **by March 2** of the year after the calendar year covered | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |
| **Worker medical and exposure records** | Health records for employees exposed to hazards | Retain for the period required by the specific record type (varies by exposure) | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |
| **Worker training records** | Proof that workers were trained on safety and hazards | Keep available for **review by workers** as required | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |
| **Fatalities, hospitalizations, amputations, eye loss** | Must be reported to OSHA at the time of event | **Within 8 hours** for fatalities; **within 24 hours** for hospitalizations, amputations, or eye loss | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |
| **Infection‑related incidents** | Record infectious diseases and fatalities | Same timing as general fatalities and hospitalizations (8 h for fatality, 24 h for hospitalization) | [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=48) |
| **Other OSHA‑specific records** | Depending on your industry, may include lock‑out/tag‑out logs, respirator programs, noise‑monitoring logs, etc. | Keep as long as applicable (often 5 years) | [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=50), [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=64) |

### Quick checklist of common safety‑related records

- **Incident logs (Forms 300/301)** – keep for 5 years.  
- **Annual summary (Form 300‑A)** – keep for 5 years.  
- **Training certificates** – keep as long as the training is required.  
- **Medical/health screening records** – keep for the required period (often years, depending on exposure).  
- **Special injury types (infectious disease, noise‑induced hearing loss, etc.)** – record on Forms 300/301 and keep for 5 years.  

If you’re a small shop with fewer than 10 workers overall last year, you may be **partially exempt** from some injury/illness recordkeeping but you still must **report** any fatalities, hospitalizations, amputations, and eye loss.  [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14)

---

**Bottom line:**  
1. A safety program saves money and protects people.  
2. Keep injury/illness logs, incident reports, and annual summaries for **5 years**; file electronic copies by **March 2** if required; report serious events within **8 or 24 hours**.  
3. Maintain training, medical, and other OSHA‑specific records for the periods required by law (usually 5 years or whatever the specific regulation says).  

These records not only help you stay compliant, but they give you the data you need to spot problems, improve procedures, and keep your business safe and successful.  [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15)[[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14)[[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=48)

runs.question: how do i register a trademark
runs.answer:
To register a trademark, you can choose either a **state‑level** or a **federal (U.S. Patent and Trademark Office, USPTO) registration**.  
1. **Decide where to register** – state registration gives you rights only within that state, while federal registration gives nationwide protection.  
2. **Search the trademark database first** to make sure the mark you want isn’t already taken [[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=10)(http://sdsos.gov/)] (you can do this through the Secretary of State’s site or the USPTO website).  
3. **File the application**:  
   * **State filing** – submit through the Secretary of State in your state; e.g., in South Dakota you can call (605) 773‑2797 or visit https://sdsos.gov/.  
   * **Federal filing** – submit through the USPTO by calling (703) 308‑HELP or (800) 786‑9199, or use the USPTO website at www.uspto.gov.  

Follow the instructions on the appropriate website, include all required documents, and pay the filing fee. The agency will review and, if approved, issue the trademark registration.



**Sources:**
1. [sba_business_planning_guide.pdf (Page 10)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=10)
